title: Which Party Fits the Bible More?
subtitle: A straight answer to a loaded question, and the test it sets for you.

sections.title: The Question Everyone Wants Answered
sections.body:
People do not ask which party fits the Bible because they are confused. They ask because they want to be confirmed. The question is not really a question. It wants a verdict that lets the asker rest. Tell me my side is God's side. Tell me the people across the aisle are not just wrong but disobedient. We have all wanted this. I have wanted this, standing in a voting booth, wanting the ballot to mean more than it could.

That hunger is the first thing worth examining, because it reveals what we have already done. We have taken a kingdom that judges every throne and tried to seat it behind one of ours. Remember the garden the night before the cross. Peter drew a sword to defend his Lord, struck the high priest's servant, and his Lord told him to put it back, for all who take the sword will perish by it. That is the scene to keep in front of you. The one we want to enlist in our coalition is the one who refused to be defended by the very weapon every coalition reaches for. The demand for a clean answer is not piety. It is the old temptation to make God a member of our coalition rather than the one before whom our coalition stands.

So here is the honest answer, and the rest of this essay is only the showing of the work. It depends entirely on which issues you weight, because Scripture weights them all. On one cluster the right sits nearer the text. On another the left sits nearer. And a Christian who reads the whole book ends up without a party, cross-pressured, politically homeless. That homelessness is not a failure of conviction. It is what it costs to follow a Lord who would not let the sword be drawn even for him.

sections.title: Where the Right Sits Nearer
sections.body:
On the unborn, the right sits nearer the text, and we should say it plainly without flinching. The Scriptures speak of the child known in the womb, knit together in secret, called before formed. A people commanded again and again not to shed innocent blood cannot treat the smallest and most defenseless life as a private matter of convenience. The conservative insistence that this hidden life has weight, that it cannot be ended for the comfort of the strong, lands closer to the heart of a God who hears the cry of those who have no voice.

On marriage and the family, the conservative instinct to protect the covenant between husband and wife, and to see children as a gift to be received within it rather than a project to be engineered, tracks a pattern the Bible treats as woven into creation. On religious liberty, the refusal to let the state press the conscience, to leave the church free to be the church and not an arm of the government, guards something the early Christians died to keep. They would not call Caesar Lord. The right's suspicion of a state that wants that title is not paranoia. It is memory.

And on that suspicion itself, the warning against an all-powerful state, the conservative reading of Scripture is not wrong to be afraid. The Bible knows what Pharaoh does, what Babylon does, what the beast in Revelation does when a government decides it answers to no one above it. The state that wants Caesar's title wants Caesar's sword behind it, and a faith that has watched empires demand worship knows that sword by sight. A faith with that memory has every reason to distrust concentrated power. I say all of this as someone who does not vote a straight conservative ticket. I say it because it is true, and because if I cannot say it, I have already lost the argument I am about to make.

sections.title: Where the Left Sits Nearer
sections.body:
On the poor, the left sits nearer the text, and the conservative who cannot admit it has not read the prophets. The Bible mentions the poor more than almost anything else it mentions. It commands gleaning laws and jubilee, it indicts the rich who feast while Lazarus starves at the gate, it warns the nation that grinds the face of the needy. Walter Brueggemann spent his life on this point, that the prophet is captive to no king's court and speaks a word the throne did not commission. Amos was no party operative. He was a herdsman who walked into the royal sanctuary and told the powerful their feasts made God sick. The political tradition that insists a society be measured by what happens to its weakest, that refuses to call a person's hunger their own fault, stands inside a thunder that runs from Amos to the Magnificat.

On the immigrant and the refugee, the command could not be more direct. Love the stranger, for you were strangers. Do not mistreat the foreigner among you. A holy family fled to Egypt as refugees from a king killing children, and the church that worships that child cannot treat the fleeing stranger as a threat to be repelled first and pitied never. On racial dignity, the conviction that every person carries the image of God, that the long American sin of treating some image-bearers as less is a sin and not a grievance to be managed, sits squarely on the first page of Genesis. On the care of creation, the charge to keep the garden and not strip it bare is older than any party.

And on the worker, the one who labors and is not paid, the Scriptures are loud where we are quiet. Do not hold back the wages of the hired hand overnight. The cry of the harvesters has reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. The left's instinct that power left unchecked will exploit the one who has only his hands to sell is not envy dressed as ethics. It is, on this cluster, the prophets' own complaint. And yet the prophet who indicts the throne is not auditioning to sit on it. The same kingdom that judges the right's love of order judges the left's faith in its own program. It will not be carried by any coalition, not even one marching under the prophets' words. I am a conservative on more days than not, and I cannot read these pages and keep my comfort.

sections.title: Why No Party Fits
sections.body:
Here is the trap that springs once both clusters are laid on the table. Scripture weights all of it. It does not give us a ranking that conveniently sorts into one platform. The same God who guards the unborn guards the immigrant. The same book that fears the all-powerful state commands a fierce concern for the poor that no purely private charity has ever delivered at scale. The clusters cannot be reconciled into a single ticket, because no party in this country has built one. Each has taken half of the Bible's concern and called it the whole.

This is why the faithful reader ends up homeless. Tim Keller argued that a Christian can belong fully to neither party, that the attempt to map biblical conviction onto a partisan platform always requires amputating the parts that do not fit. He was right, and the amputation is the tell. When a Christian finds that every one of his convictions happens to line up with one party's platform, top to bottom, the most likely explanation is not that the party is righteous. It is that the party has become the lens, and the Bible the thing read through it.

So the cross-pressure is not a problem to be solved. It is a sign of life. It means the text is still speaking with a voice your tribe has not yet silenced. The Christian walks into the public square carrying convictions that embarrass both coalitions, voting always for a fraction and never for a fulfillment, grieving the ballot even as he casts it. That is not fence-sitting. Fence-sitting is having no convictions. This is having too many for any one party to hold.

Now watch yourself. If reading both halves left you feeling balanced and fair, distrust that feeling. The reader most at risk is not the partisan who threw the essay down at his own side's critique. It is the one who read the critique of his own side and felt relieved that the other side got it too. That relief is the symptom. The mechanism is not out there in the parties. It is in you, reading this, right now, in the part of you that already knows which side this paragraph is really about.

sections.title: The Real Test
sections.body:
So I will not tell you how to vote. I will not crown a party, because the King I serve did not run on either ticket and will judge both. The real question was never which party fits the Bible more. The real question is whether the Bible or your tribe is your master, and there is a way to find out that no slogan can fake.

Here it is. Can you name, out loud, in front of people who will not thank you for it, where your own side is unbiblical? Not where the other side is. Anyone can do that, and doing it costs nothing. Can the conservative say without hedging that the way his party often treats the poor and the stranger is a betrayal of the prophets, and the progressive that the way her party often treats the unborn and the conscience is a betrayal of the same God? The ease or the impossibility of that sentence is the whole test.

Because if you cannot find a single place where your party is wrong, you have not discovered a righteous party. You have discovered your god. I have caught myself defending the indefensible because my team did it, excusing in my own coalition what I would have called sin in the other, and the catching always feels like a small death. It is supposed to. That is what an idol feels like when it is pried loose. And it comes back, in the end, to a sword and a hand told to sheathe it. The Lord we keep trying to arm is the one who would not be defended by force the night they came for him. He will not be carried into the public square on the point of our certainty either. The Bible fits no party. It was never trying to. It is trying to fit you. And it will not stop pressing until it does.
